response.answer: Adopt WordPiece tokenization and reversible normalization for unambiguous token-IoU. Use special prefix `##` for subtoken continuations. Ensure consistent subtoken-to-token mapping.

results.content: # [](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/tokenizer_summary#tokenization-algorithms)Tokenization algorithms. ## [](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/tokenizer_summary#byte-pair-encoding-bpe)Byte pair encoding (BPE). [Byte pair encoding](https://huggingface.co/papers/1508.07909) (BPE) is the most popular tokenization algorithm in Transformers, used by models like [Llama](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/model_doc/llama), [Gemma](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/model_doc/gemma), [Qwen2](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/model_doc/qwen2), and more. [GPT](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/model_doc/openai-gpt) uses BPE with a vocabulary size of 40,478 (478 base tokens + 40,000 merges). ### [](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/tokenizer_summary#byte-level-bpe)Byte-level BPE. [GPT-2](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/model_doc/gpt2) uses byte-level BPE with a vocabulary size of 50,257 (256 byte tokens + 50,000 merges + special end-of-text token). ## [](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/tokenizer_summary#unigram)Unigram. [Unigram](https://huggingface.co/papers/1804.10959) is the second most popular tokenization algorithm in Transformers, used by models like [T5](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/model_doc/t5), [BigBird](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/model_doc/big_bird), [Pegasus](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/model_doc/pegasus), and more. ## [](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/tokenizer_summary#sentencepiece)SentencePiece. [SentencePiece](https://huggingface.co/papers/1808.06226) is a tokenization library that applies BPE or Unigram directly on raw text. ## [](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/tokenizer_summary#wordpiece)WordPiece. [WordPiece](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/research.google.com/en//pubs/archive/37842.pdf) is the tokenization algorithm for BERT-family models like [DistilBERT](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/model_doc/distilbert) and [Electra](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/model_doc/electra). It’s similar to [BPE](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/tokenizer_summary#byte-pair-encoding-bpe) and iteratively merges pairs from the bottom up, but differs in how it selects pairs. ## [](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/tokenizer_summary#word-level-tokenization)Word-level tokenization. ## [](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/tokenizer_summary#character-level-tokenization)Character-level tokenization. ## [](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/tokenizer_summary#resources)Resources. results.title: WordPiece Tokenization Algorithm
results.content: # WordPiece Tokenization. WordPiece tokenization is an approach for building large vocabularies, developed at Google and notably used for models like BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) and its variants. Unlike Byte Pair Encoding (BPE), which merges the most frequent pairs of tokens, WordPiece's merge criterion is based on maximizing the likelihood of the training data, rather than raw frequency counts. WordPiece chooses the pair (say, AAA and BBB) such that merging them into a single token ABABAB results in the largest increase in the likelihood of the training corpus, assuming a unigram language model over the tokens. Like many BPE implementations, WordPiece typically handles subwords within a word by adding a special prefix (commonly `##`) to tokens that represent continuations of a word. The primary distinction between WordPiece and BPE is the criterion for merging tokens: BPE uses frequency, while WordPiece uses corpus likelihood maximization (or a related score).

results.title: Normalization and pre-tokenization · Hugging Face
results.content: # Normalization and pre-tokenization. Before splitting a text into subtokens (according to its model), the tokenizer performs two steps: *normalization* and *pre-tokenization*. SentencePiece is a tokenization algorithm for the preprocessing of text that you can use with any of the models we will see in the next three sections. Used in conjunction with the Unigram algorithm (see section 7), it doesn’t even require a pre-tokenization step, which is very useful for languages where the space character is not used (like Chinese or Japanese). The other main feature of SentencePiece is *reversible tokenization*: since there is no special treatment of spaces, decoding the tokens is done simply by concatenating them and replacing the `_`s with spaces — this results in the normalized text. In the following sections, we’ll dive into the three main subword tokenization algorithms: BPE (used by GPT-2 and others), WordPiece (used for example by BERT), and Unigram (used by T5 and others).

results.title: Advanced Tokenization Methods (BPE, WordPiece)
results.content: Originally developed as a data compression algorithm, Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) was adapted for NLP tokenization to manage vocabulary size effectively while handling word variations. `{h, u, g, </w>, e, r, s, ug}`. `{h, u, g, </w>, e, r, s, ug, hug}`. `{h, u, g, </w>, e, r, s, ug, hug, ge}`. **Tokenizing New Text:** To tokenize a new word (e.g., "hugging"), BPE applies the learned merge rules greedily. If a subword unit does not represent the start of an original word, it's typically prefixed with a special symbol, often `##` (e.g., "tokenization" might become `['token', '##ization']`). Both BPE and WordPiece effectively reduce vocabulary size compared to word-level tokens, handle OOV words by breaking them down into known subwords, and capture morphological relationships (e.g., "run", "running" likely share the "run" subword). Libraries like Hugging Face's `transformers` abstract away many of the implementation details, allowing you to easily load and use the appropriate tokenizer for a given model (e.g., `BertTokenizer` uses WordPiece, `GPT2Tokenizer` uses BPE).

Title: Normalization and pre-tokenization - Hugging Face LLM Course
# Normalization and pre-tokenization. Before we dive more deeply into the three most common subword tokenization algorithms used with Transformer models (Byte-Pair Encoding [BPE], WordPiece, and Unigram), we’ll first take a look at the preprocessing that each tokenizer applies to text. Before splitting a text into subtokens (according to its model), the tokenizer performs two steps: *normalization* and *pre-tokenization*. ## Pre-tokenization. As we will see in the next sections, a tokenizer cannot be trained on raw text alone. As we saw in Chapter 2, a word-based tokenizer can simply split a raw text into words on whitespace and punctuation. For a last example, let’s have a look at the T5 tokenizer, which is based on the SentencePiece algorithm:. Like the GPT-2 tokenizer, this one keeps spaces and replaces them with a specific token (`_`), but the T5 tokenizer only splits on whitespace, not punctuation. We’ll begin with a quick look at the broadly widely applicable SentencePiece; then, over the next three sections, we’ll examine how the three main algorithms used for subword tokenization work. SentencePiece is a tokenization algorithm for the preprocessing of text that you can use with any of the models we will see in the next three sections. Used in conjunction with the Unigram algorithm (see section 7), it doesn’t even require a pre-tokenization step, which is very useful for languages where the space character is not used (like Chinese or Japanese). The other main feature of SentencePiece is *reversible tokenization*: since there is no special treatment of spaces, decoding the tokens is done simply by concatenating them and replacing the `_`s with spaces — this results in the normalized text. In the following sections, we’ll dive into the three main subword tokenization algorithms: BPE (used by GPT-2 and others), WordPiece (used for example by BERT), and Unigram (used by T5 and others). | Encoding | Splits a word into characters and applies the merges learned during training | Finds the longest subword starting from the beginning that is in the vocabulary, then does the same for the rest of the word | Finds the most likely split into tokens, using the scores learned during training |.
